Issued at 341 PM CDT Tue Aug 18 2026

Shower and storm complex that dropped southeastward out of Nebraska 
today has a large role in how the mesoscale environment has evolved 
today. The expansive cloud cover associated with this limited the 
boundary layer's ability to destabilize through much of the 
afternoon, which stopped the conditional threat for stronger storms 
this afternoon. We currently have a series of H5 vort maxima that 
have been traversing the Central Plains and parts of the upper 
Midwest over the past several hours. This is downstream from a mid-
level ridge present over the southwestern CONUS.

Differential cyclonic vorticity advection has remained present over 
the Central Plains, allowing the surface cyclone to deepen through 
the day and extend pressure falls eastward into the lower Missouri 
River Valley. The earlier outflow boundaries have washed out over 
the past couple of hours. The winds are now returning to a southerly 
direction after becoming northerly with the series of outflows from 
this morning's activity. This will attempt to restart theta-e 
advection through the afternoon, but, much of northwestern and north-
central Missouri remains under overcast skies, which will limit 
instability and will play a role in the evolution of the 
late/overnight activity. However, recent satellite trends as of 20z 
is showing clearing in portions of eastern Kansas, perhaps an small 
area of subsidence that has developed with the enhanced mid-level 
flow over the past 24 hours. The next few hours late this afternoon 
and into the early evening should allow for an instability axis to 
develop over Central Kansas, perhaps as far east as the Flint Hills. 
Areas further east may struggle to destabilize, at least with 
respect to MLCAPE and surface-based CAPE parcels. As the cyclone 
deepens and slowly shifts eastward, low-level convergence should 
continue to increase through late evening, with the low-level jet 
set to ramp up as well. This will become the focus for storm 
initiation for the remainder of the night. With current instability 
trends, current expectation is for CI more in eastern KS, but should 
quickly expand eastward into the lower Missouri River Valley. Some 
cells may be able to go as early as 00z in central Kansas, but for 
our forecast area, may hold off until 03-04z for expansion. This 
timing and location of CI will have implications for storm mode, as 
well as the associated hazards. Given that there does not appear to 
be enough for sufficient surface CAPE to develop in our eastern 
Kansas counties over to Central Missouri, the opportunity for 
supercells will be more confined to Kansas, just west of the 
forecast area. However, supercells may be able to travel eastward, 
especially if they latch onto the cold front, potentially hitting 
our western zones, and may get close to the KC metro. If a supercell 
is able to develop, large hail (in excess of 2") is possible along 
with strong RFD winds. If the supercell remains surface based, it 
will present a tornado threat, though that threat seems to diminish 
the further east of the KS Flint Hills (given that 0-3km CAPE will 
be hard to come by and limited stretching potential). There will be 
plenty of kinematic support even into Central MO, but the 
thermodynamic environment remains in question. Low-level hodographs 
are expected to curve, especially close to the cold front where low-
level SRH could easily exceed 150 m^2/s^2. The more likely scenario 
for our forecast area is upscale growth into an organized MCS. While 
new cell development may have elevated bases, mid-level lapse rates 
and MUCAPE profiles will allow for strong updrafts, with plenty of 
wind shear to help organize the activity. This would support the 
development of strong cold pools this evening, with strong negative 
buoyancy supporting damaging wind gusts, potentially with some near 
70 MPH. New cores may briefly pose a hail threat before congealing 
with other cells or being ingested into an MCS. The kinematic 
environment could be favorable for attempting to support meso vortex 
generation if the mode should become more linear, but unsure if 0-
3km CAPE would be high enough to help with stretching that to the 
surface to present any QLCS tornado threat. The most robust activity 
is favored between 1a-5a overnight (06z-10z). Where a mature MCS 
tracks and propagates still remains uncertain, as this will largely 
depend on where the best CAPE axis can develop. Given the steering 
flow, this is likely to track toward the south-southeast, but at 
what point does it start to take on this motion remains the main the 
questions. The bulk of the activity should exit the forecast area 
after 12z.
